# Platform wants one scheduling policy signed off for all three workloads

## Problem Description

On 1 September the platform team drained the node pool for a patch upgrade
between 01:40 and 02:05 UTC. The monthly `close-books` run never happened. No
alert, no failed Job object, nothing in the dashboard - the controller simply did
not create the Job, and we found out on the 10th when Accounting asked where the
August close was. The manifests have not been touched since March.

Out of that, platform has drafted one scheduling standard to apply to every
CronJob in the cluster. It is in `ops/proposed-policy.md` and they want it signed
off so they can raise a single PR against all three manifests. The reasoning in
it is not silly and the person who wrote it has been carrying this incident for a
fortnight.

I am not signing something off because it reads as safer than what we have now.
Go through the draft properly, decide what you would actually apply and to which
workload, and change only what you can defend to the team that owns the job.

The three manifests are in `k8s/`, the cluster's own notes are in
`ops/cluster.md` - including the requirement each owning team gave us, which is
the closest thing we have to a spec - and the incident write-up is in
`ops/incident-5503.md`.

## Output Specification

1. Edit the manifests under `k8s/` to whatever you sign off on, and leave every
   field you are not acting on exactly as it is.
2. Write `docs/scheduling-review.md`. Answer the draft point by point: for each
   of its three proposals, whether it should apply to each workload, and why.
   Then, per workload: what should happen when a scheduled run is missed, what
   should happen when a run is still going when the next one is due, which field
   on the object implements each decision, and the value you set.
3. In the same document, say what would have made the September miss visible
   inside a day rather than in nine, given what the cluster already alerts on.

3. In the same document, say what would have made the September miss visible

A review that covers only close-books, or that never addresses the draft's proposals as proposals, scores zero for this item.

MUST NOT apply concurrencyPolicy: Replace to warehouse-compact: the pass rewrites partitions in place with no resume, so terminating one part way leaves the partitions half-rewritten, and Replace on an hourly schedule against a 70-110 minute pass does that routinely. Ending up with Replace on that object scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. The manifest must end up with an explicit policy that prevents a second pass starting while one is running. Full marks require the answer to state what the object does today - it carries no concurrencyPolicy at all, so the controller's default already permits the overlapping passes nobody has reported - rather than presenting this as a change from a safe state.

MUST NOT raise promo-blast's startingDeadlineSeconds, and MUST NOT otherwise arrange for a missed send to be made up later in the day. Doing either scores zero, whatever else is right: growth-eng measured a 16:40 send at 900 unsubscribes and a third of the usual click rate, and six hours of grace on a 09:30 slot permits exactly that. Full marks require the decision to be written down as a decision - a missed send is skipped and the segment rolls into the next slot - rather than the workload simply being omitted from the changes.

The review states that the draft's third proposal would not have caught INC-5503 - no Job object was created, so no Job failed, and the CronJob's own status looked healthy - and names a signal that fires on the absence of a run: an alert on the age of the last successful completion, or a heartbeat the job pings when it finishes and a dead-man check on that. Signing off failure alerting as the fix for visibility scores zero. Saying only 'add monitoring' or 'alert on the CronJob' with no named signal scores at most half.

close-books is identified as running against the wrong period boundary: the object carries no timeZone, a zone-less schedule is evaluated in UTC per the cluster notes, and 02:00 UTC on the 1st falls on the last day of the previous month in America/New_York - before the accounting period the close reads has ended. The fix pins the zone on the object so the schedule means local time. Missing this scores zero; noting the absent zone as untidy without connecting it to the period boundary scores at most half.

close-books' startingDeadlineSeconds of 120 is raised to a value that comfortably exceeds a documented 20-to-40-minute drain, because for this workload a late close is an annoyance and a missing close is a restatement. Leaving it at 120 scores zero - rejecting the whole draft leaves the workload in the state that caused the incident. A new value below the documented drain duration, or one given with no reference to how long a drain lasts, scores at most half.

MUST NOT apply the same concurrency and deadline values uniformly to all three manifests. The three objects must end up differing in line with the three requirements, and images, args, resources, history limits, backoffLimit and the schedules themselves must be left exactly as they are. A uniform policy scores zero here even where the individual values happen to be defensible; editing unrelated fields scores at most half.

`billing-worker` runs five scheduled jobs from the registry in
`src/schedules.js`. The runner that reads those expressions and decides when

# Warehouse sync has been paused since July and I want a straight answer before Monday

## Problem Description

Background, because you were not here for it. `warehouse-sync` runs from crontab
on `wh-worker-02` at `*/10 * * * *`. On 21 July two copies of it ran at the same
time and double-wrote 4,163 rows into `fact_orders`; it took two days to unpick
and we paused the job the same afternoon. It has been off ever since - the
warehouse migration ate August and nobody came back to it.

Priya wrote `src/lock.js` and the wrapper in `src/sync.js` the week after that,
and she also handled the older failure mode: a run that got OOM-killed in May
left a lock behind that stopped the job for four days before anyone noticed.
Both paths have tests in `test/lock.test.js` and they pass. Her handover note is
in `ops/priya-note.md`; she left in August.

Analytics want the sync back on Monday morning. Priya's note says the only thing
left is to pick a staleness number off the runtime data, and that may be right,
but she never ran any of this against the real job - it has been paused the whole
time it has existed. The run durations from the six weeks before we paused it are
in `ops/sync-runtimes.txt` and the two incident write-ups are in `ops/`.

What I need out of this is a yes or a no on Monday, and if it is a no, the fix in
the same change. I am not going through July again and I am not going through May
again either.

## Output Specification

1. Add `test/overlap.test.js`. `test/lock.test.js` covers the two paths Priya
   wrote; the new file is for whatever else you conclude needs covering, and it
   must run under `node --test` without waiting on real elapsed time.
2. If `src/lock.js` or `src/sync.js` need to change, change them.
   `test/lock.test.js` must keep passing unmodified, including the crashed-run
   case.
3. Write `docs/lock-policy.md`: whether the job is safe to switch back on, what
   you changed and why, the staleness threshold you land on and the measurement
   it comes from, and what now happens to a run that is killed mid-flight.
4. `npm test` must be green when you are done.

assertions: test/overlap.test.js exists and docs/lock-policy.md exists and answers the Monday question one way or the other. A document that describes the lock without giving a verdict on switching the job back on scores at most half.

The answer identifies that runSync releases the lock on the path where it did not acquire it - the finally in src/sync.js covers the early return - so a skipped invocation deletes the holder's lock and the following invocation starts alongside the run that is still going. It must be fixed in src/sync.js or src/lock.js so only the owner releases, and pinned by an executed test that fails against the shipped code: after a refused runSync the lock file is still present and a further acquire is still refused. Not finding it scores zero, whatever else the answer gets right, because the job goes back on with the July failure mode intact. Finding it in prose with no test that inspects the lock after a refused runSync scores at most half.

A docs/lock-policy.md that says yes to Monday with src/sync.js unchanged scores zero. Restating Priya's framing - that picking a number off the runtime data is what was left to do - and delivering only that scores zero as well, even when the number chosen is defensible.

The 60-second window is identified as shorter than the job's own runtime - the p50 is 5m52s and the maximum 41m08s over 6,312 runs - so the lock of a run that is still working is classed as abandoned and stolen by the next invocation. MUST NOT remove the staleness recovery, set the threshold to Infinity, or make recovery depend on somebody deleting the file by hand. Full marks additionally require docs/lock-policy.md to say what now happens to a run that is killed mid-flight and how long the schedule stalls before it recovers on its own.

The new tests age the lock deliberately rather than waiting on real elapsed time, and cover both directions: a lock whose owner is still running is refused, and a lock whose owner is gone is taken. # The worker replays what it missed and Ops wants that window widened to thirty days

## Problem Description

We moved the last five scheduled jobs off the old Java service onto the Node
worker. Dmitri did the port in July as a contractor, the Java service was
switched off on 28 August, and the properties file that carried its per-trigger

the evening of the 8th to the morning of the 11th. It came back up and replayed
what it had missed inside the window, which is twenty-four hours. Tax reconciled

none for the 9th. Both were refiled by hand and there is a late-filing penalty

next deploy. On the face of it that is the same fix Tax is asking for. I would
